title: Proof
body_md: As differentially-defined functions are solutions of ODEs, the results presented in this article extend upon earlier works concerning the proof theory of ODEs \cite{DBLP:conf/lics/Platzer12a, DBLP:journals/jacm/PlatzerT20, platzer2024axiomatizationcompactinitialvalue}, which is relatively unexplored compared to the computability/complexity of theory of ODEs \cite{Pouly_Bournez_2020, DBLP:journals/tocl/Ratschan06, Graca_Zhong_Buescu_2009, DBLP:journals/jc/BournezGGP23, Gao_Avigad_Clarke_2012, DBLP:journals/toct/KawamuraC12}. Earlier works only consider either \emph{exact} completeness \cite{DBLP:journals/jacm/PlatzerT20, platzer2024axiomatizationcompactinitialvalue} without approximations or completeness relative to some non-computable oracle \cite{Platzer_2012}, and therefore do not provide computable axiomatizations that are approximately complete. In particular, earlier works that give computable axiomatizations only concern the fragment of $\mathbb{R}_D$ with at most one quantifier \cite{platzer2024axiomatizationcompactinitialvalue}, whereas the results in this article allow for arbitrary (bounded) quantifiers and are therefore much more general.

label: thm: stone weierstrass for IVPs
title: Theorem
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{thm: stone weierstrass for IVPs}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $f(x) \in \mathbb{Q}^n[x]$ be a polynomial vector field with rational coefficients, $X \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ rational initial conditions, $t_0, T \in \mathbb{Q}$ a rational interval with $t_0 \leq T$. Further suppose that the solution to initial value problem
    \begin{align*}
        &x' = f(x)\\
        &x(t_0) = X
    \end{align*}
    does not exhibit finite time blow-up on $[t_0, T]$. Then for all $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{Q}^+$, there (computably) exists some $\theta(t) \in \mathbb{Q}^n[t]$ such that the following formula is provable in $\text{\upshape\textsf{d{\kern-0.05em}L}}\xspace$:
    \[x = X \& t = t_0 \rightarrow [#x' = f(x), t' = 1 \& t \leq T]#\left\lVertx - \theta(t)\right\rVert^2 \leq \varepsilon^2\]
head: environment
name: Stone-Weierstrass {}

label: thm: stone weierstrass for functions
title: Theorem
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{thm: stone weierstrass for functions}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $h(t)$ be a differentially-defined function, and $T \in \mathbb{Q}^+$ be arbitrary. Then for all $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{Q}^+$, there (computably) exists some $p(t) \in \mathbb{Q}[t]$ such that the following formula is provable in $\text{\upshape\textsf{d{\kern-0.05em}L}}\xspace$:
    \begin{equation}
        \if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{fml: error bound}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
        -T \leq t \leq T \rightarrow \lvertp(t) - h(t)\rvert < \varepsilon
    \end{equation}

name: Stone-Weierstrass for Differentially-Defined Functions

body_md: Since differentially-defined functions are solutions to IVPs, it suffices to apply Theorem \ref{thm: stone weierstrass for IVPs} on both the positive and negative time regions to obtain the desired approximation, see Appendix \ref{app: proofs} for a complete proof.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $x \in \mathbb{R}$ be any real number, a $\it{name}$ for $x$ is a sequence of rationals $(q_i)_i \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$ such that
    \[\boldsymbol{\forall} i \in \mathbb{N}~(\lvertq_i - x\rvert < 2^{-i})\]
    This definition naturally extends to $\mathbb{R}^n$ by requiring names to reside in $\mathbb{Q}^n$ and using the standard Euclidean norm. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we denote the set of all names of $x$ as $\Gamma(x)$.

title: Definition
body_md: An \emph{oracle machine $M$} is a Turing machine that allows for an additional one-way read-only input tape that represents some input oracle used. The machine is allowed to read this input tape up to arbitrary, but finite, lengths.
head: environment

label: def: computable function
title: Definition
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{def: computable function}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is \emph{computable} if there is some oracle machine $M$ such that 
    \[\boldsymbol{\forall}x \in \mathbb{R}^n~\boldsymbol{\forall} p \in \Gamma(x)~((M^p(i))_i \in \Gamma(f(x)))\]
    I.e. $M$ maps names of $x$ to names of $f(x)$ for all $x \in E$.

name: Computable function

title: Definition
body_md:
The following standard notations will be used. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ denotes the set of all intervals with rational endpoints, i.e.
        \[\mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q} = \{[\underline{a}, \overline{a}] ~\vert~ \underline{a} \leq \overline{a} \in \mathbb{Q}\}\]
        \item $\mathbb{R} = \langle \mathbb{R}, 0, 1, +, \cdot, \geq, > \rangle$ is always treated as a real-closed field. The logical symbol `$=$' is defined as $x = y \iff x \geq y \& y \geq x$. We assume without loss of generality that the only relation symbols used are $\{\geq, >\}$ and atomic formulas are of the form $t \succeq 0$ for $\succeq~\in \{\geq, >\}$ and $t$ a term. 
        \item $\mathbb{R}_D$ is the extension of $\mathbb{R}$ with all differentially-defined functions with provable global existence, $\mathbb{R}_C$ is the extension of $\mathbb{R}$ with all univariate computable functions.
        \item $\mathcal{L}_R$ denotes the standard language of real-closed fields, assumed to include all rationals, definable functions and the relation symbol $\geq$ without loss of generality. $\mathcal{L}_D$ denotes the language of $\mathbb{R}_D$ and $\mathcal{L}_C$ denotes the language of $\mathbb{R}_C$. 
        \item For a language $\mathcal{L}$, $\text{Fml}(\mathcal{L})$/$\text{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ denotes the set of all $\mathcal{L}$ formulas/sentences and $\text{Term}(\mathcal{L})$ denotes the set of all terms. For a formula $\varphi \in \text{Fml}(\mathcal{L})$, $\text{Term}(\varphi)$ denotes all terms appearing in $\varphi$ and $\text{Term}_{\text{F}}(\varphi)$ denotes all function terms (i.e. terms of the form $f(e)$). A term $t \in \text{Term}(\mathcal{L})$ is \emph{function-free} if it does not contain function symbols. By a slight abuse of notation, a term $e(\vec{x}) \in \text{Term}(\mathcal{L})$ is also identified with the function $\vec{x} \mapsto \left\llbracket e(\vec{x}) \right\rrbracket$. $\text{Fml}(\mathcal{L}_R)$ is also denoted as $\text{FOL}_{\mathbb{R}}$. 
        \item For $\mathcal{L} \in \{\mathcal{L}_R, \mathcal{L}_C, \mathcal{L}_D\}$, $\psi \in \text{Fml}(\mathcal{L})$, $a, b \in \text{Term}(\mathcal{L})$ and $Q \in \{\exists, \forall\}$ a quantifier, the bounded quantifier $Q^{[a, b]}~\psi(x, \vec{y})$ is defined as:
        \begin{align*}
            &\exists^{[a, b]}x~\psi(x, \vec{y}) = \exists x \left(a \leq x \& x \leq b \& \psi(x, y)\right)\\
            &\forall^{[a, b]}x~\psi(x, \vec{y}) = \forall x \left(a \leq x \& x \leq b \rightarrow \psi(x, y)\right)
        \end{align*}
        \item For $\mathcal{L} \in \{\mathcal{L}_R, \mathcal{L}_C, \mathcal{L}_D\}$, a formula $\varphi \in \text{Fml}(\mathcal{L})$ is \emph{bounded} if
        \[\varphi(\vec{x}) \equiv Q_1^{I_1}y_1Q_2^{I_2}y_2\cdots Q_n^{I_n}~y_n\psi(\vec{x}, y_1, \cdots, y_n)\]
        where $Q_i \in \{\exists, \forall\}$ denotes the $i$-th quantifier, $I_i = [a_i, b_i]$ are closed intervals that could potentially depend on variables appearing before $y_i$ and $\psi(\vec{x}, y_1, \cdots, y_n)$ is a quantifier free formula in conjunctive normal form. We assume without loss of generality that all (bounded) formulas are in this normal form. 
        \item For $\mathcal{L} \in \{\mathcal{L}_R, \mathcal{L}_C, \mathcal{L}_D\}$, $\succeq~\in \{\geq, >\}$ $\text{Fml}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L})$/$\text{Sent}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L})$ denotes the formulas/sentences that only contain the relation $\succeq$.
        \item For a language $\mathcal{L} \in \{\mathcal{L}_R, \mathcal{L}_C, \mathcal{L}_D\}$, the set of all bounded formulas/sentences is denoted as $\text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L})$/$\text{Sent}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L})$. Note that a bounded formula $Q^{[a, b]}x\psi(x, \vec{y})$ can always be equivalently written as
        \[Q^{[a, b]}x~\psi(x, \vec{y}) \equiv Q^{[0, 1]}t~\psi(at + (1 - t)b, \vec{y})\]
        Thus, bounded formulas/sentences are assumed without loss of generality to only quantify over intervals $[a, b]$ where the terms $a, b$ do not contain function symbols. The following notations will be useful (where $\succeq~\in \{\geq, >\}$):
        \begin{align*}
            \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L}) &\coloneqq \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}) \cap \text{Fml}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L})\\
            \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L}) &\coloneqq \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}) \cap \text{Sent}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L})
        \end{align*}
        \item For $\mathcal{L} \in \{\mathcal{L}_R, \mathcal{L}_C, \mathcal{L}_D\}$ and $R$ an $\mathcal{L}$-structure, $\text{Th}(R)$ denotes the theory of $R$ and $\text{Th}_{\text{B}}(R)$ denotes the bounded fragment of $\text{Th}(R)$. Restricting the theory will also be useful (where $\succeq~\in\{\geq, >\})$:
        \begin{align*}
            \text{Th}_{\text{B}}^{\succeq}(R) &\coloneqq \text{Th}_{\text{B}}(R) \cap \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}^{\succeq}(\mathcal{L})\\
        \end{align*}
    \end{itemize}

name: Domain of bounded formulas

label: def: enclosures
title: Definition
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{def: enclosures}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{Q}^+$, and $\varphi \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$ be a bounded formula. An $\varepsilon$-enclosure of $\varphi$ is a function $I : \text{Term}(\varphi) \to \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ satisfying the following requirements. For clarity, $I(e)$ for a term $e$ is also written as
    \[I(e) = I_e = [\underline{e}, \overline{e}]\]

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For $x \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$ a free variable, $I_x$ enforces no requirements 
            \[I_x \in \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}\]
        \item For $x \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$ a bound variable introduced via the quantifier $Q^{[a, b]}x$, $I_x$ satisfies
        \[I_a \cup I_b \subseteq I_x\]
        \item For a term $t = t_1 + t_2 \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$, $I_t$ satisfies
        \[I_{t_1} + I_{t_2} \subseteq I_{t_1 + t_2}\]
        with the usual addition of intervals:
            \[[\underline{t_1}, \overline{t_1}] + [\underline{t_2}, \overline{t_2}] = [\underline{t_1} + \underline{t_2}, \overline{t_1} + \overline{t_2}]\]
        \item For a term $t = t_1\cdot t_2 \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$, $I_t$ satisfies
            \[I_{t_1} \cdot I_{t_2} \subseteq I_{t_1 \cdot t_2}\]
            with the usual multiplication of intervals:
        \[[\underline{t_1}, \overline{t_1}] \cdot [\underline{t_2}, \overline{t_2}] = [\min(\underline{t_1}\underline{t_2}, \underline{t_1}\overline{t_2}, \overline{t_1}\underline{t_2}, \overline{t_1}\overline{t_2}), \max(\underline{t_1}\underline{t_2}, \underline{t_1}\overline{t_2}, \overline{t_1}\underline{t_2}, \overline{t_1}\overline{t_2})]\]
        \item For a term $f(e) \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$, $I_{f(e)}$ satisfies
            \[f(I_e) + [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon] \subseteq I_{f(e)}\]
            where $f$ is identified with its interpretation in $\mathbb{R}_D$ and $f(I_e)$ denotes the image of $I_e$ under $f$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    $1$-enclosures are also referred to as enclosures. An $\varepsilon$-enclosure $I$ is \emph{provable} if the conditions above are provable in $\text{\upshape\textsf{d{\kern-0.05em}L}}\xspace$.
head: environment
name: $\eps$-enclosures

label: thm: compute enclosures
title: Theorem
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{thm: compute enclosures}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    For all $\varphi \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$ and $D : FV(\varphi) \to \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ a domain of $\varphi$, for all $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{Q}^+$, an $\varepsilon$-enclosure $I : \text{Term}(\varphi) \to \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ extending $D$ ($I\lvert_{FV(\varphi)} = D$) can be computed uniformly in $D, \varphi, \varepsilon$.
head: environment
name: Computable $\eps$-enclosures

title: Proof
body_md:
The desired $\varepsilon$-enclosure $I$ is constructed by induction:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For $x \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$ a free variable: 
            \[I_x = D_x\]
        \item For $x \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$ a bound variable introduced via $Q^{[a, b]}x$:
        \[I_x = [\underline{a}, \overline{b}]\]
        \item For terms $t = t_1 + t_2 \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$:
            \[I_{t} = I_{t_1} + I_{t_2}\]
        \item For terms $t = t_1\cdot t_2$:
            \[I_t = I_{t_1} \cdot I_{t_2}\]
        \item For terms $f(e) \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$, first compute rationals $p, q \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that 
        \begin{align*}
            &\lvertp - \min_{s \in I_e} f(e)\rvert < 1\\
            &\lvertq - \max_{s \in I_e} f(e)\rvert < 1
        \end{align*}
        Note that this is computable as solutions to IVPs are computable \cite{Graca_Zhong_Buescu_2009}. Define 
        \[I_{f(e)} = [p - \varepsilon - 1, q + \varepsilon + 1]\]
        it follows by construction that 
        \[f(I_e) + [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon] \subseteq [p - 1, q + 1] + [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon] = I_{f(e)}\]
    \end{itemize}
    The above construction is computable in $\varphi, \varepsilon$ and yields an $\varepsilon$-enclosure of $\varphi$, which completes the proof.
head: environment

label: thm: enclosures are provable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{thm: enclosures are provable}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\varphi \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$ be a bounded formula, $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{Q}^+$ and $I : \text{Term}(\varphi) \to \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ an $\varepsilon$-enclosure. Then $I$ is a \emph{provable} $\sfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$-enclosure for $\varphi$.
head: environment
name: $\eps$-enclosures are provable

title: Proof
body_md:
Clearly every $\varepsilon$-enclosure is an $\sfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$-enclosure, so it suffices to establish the provability claims, this is proven inductively on the structural complexity of terms. Let $I$ be an $\varepsilon$-enclosure. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For $x \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$ a free variable, no restrictions are placed on $I_x$ and therefore there is nothing to prove. 

       \item For terms of the form $t = t_1 + t_2 \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$, it suffices to notice that the condition $I_{t_1} + I_{t_2} \subseteq I_t$ is a comparison of rational intervals, therefore provable with axiom  
                                                         
                                                                                         
                                                                            
                                
                                                                                        
      
                                      
     
  \text{\irref@doqear+\vargend} 
. An identical argument also handles $t = t_1 \cdot t_2$ and bound variables.

       \item Let $f(e) \in \text{Term}(\varphi)$ be a term and $T \in \mathbb{Q}^+$ be large enough such that $I_e \subseteq [-T, T]$. Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}[t]$ be some polynomial approximation of $f$ on the interval $[-T, T]$ with provable uniform error at most $\sfrac{\varepsilon}{4}$ computed by Theorem \ref{thm: stone weierstrass for functions}. The following $\text{FOL}_{\mathbb{R}}$ formula (using standard abbreviations) is then valid by the triangle inequality and therefore provable using  
                                                         
                                                                                         
                                                                            
                                
                                                                                        
      
                                      
     
  \text{\irref@doqear+\vargend} 

       \[t \in I_e \rightarrow p(t) + [-\sfrac{3\varepsilon}{4}, \sfrac{3\varepsilon}{4}] \subseteq I_{f(e)}\]
       As $p(t)$ has \emph{provable} error at most $\sfrac{\varepsilon}{4}$, it further follows that the following formula is provable as well
       \[t \in I_e \rightarrow f(t) + [-\sfrac{\varepsilon}{2}, \sfrac{\varepsilon}{2}] \subseteq I_{f(e)}\]
       thereby completing the proof of $I$ being a provable $\sfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ enclosure. 
    \end{itemize}
    As the construction above handles all cases, the proof is complete.
head: environment

label: cor: compute provable enclosures
title: Corollary
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout

label: remark: analogy for delta decidability
title: Remark
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{remark: analogy for delta decidability}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    For a bounded formula $\varphi \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$, $\mathcal{A}^\forall_{\mathcal{F}}\left(\varphi, \delta\right)$ can also be viewed as \emph{strengthening} $\varphi$ by an amount of $\delta$, and $\mathcal{A}^\exists_{\mathcal{F}}\left(\varphi(\vec{x}), \delta\right)$ as \emph{weakening} $\varphi$ by an amount of $\delta$. As Theorem \ref{thm: proof rules for delta perturbations} establishes, it is indeed the case that both $\mathcal{A}^\forall_{\mathcal{F}}\left(\varphi, \delta\right) \rightarrow \varphi$ and $\varphi \rightarrow \mathcal{A}^\exists_{\mathcal{F}}\left(\varphi, \delta\right)$ are provably valid for appropriate choices of $\mathcal{F}$ (Definition \ref{def: admissible approximants}).

label: def: admissible approximants
title: Definition
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{def: admissible approximants}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\varphi \in \text{Fml}_B(\mathcal{L}_D)$ be a bounded formula, $I : \text{Term}(\varphi) \to \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ an enclosure and $\mathcal{F} : \text{Term}_F(\varphi) \to \text{FOL}_{\mathbb{R}}$ an approximation. The norm of $\mathcal{F}$ relative to enclosure $I$, denoted $\left\lVert\mathcal{F}\right\rVert_I$, is defined as:
    \[ \left\lVert\mathcal{F}\right\rVert_I = \max_{f(e) \in \text{Term}_{\text{F}}(\varphi)} \left\lVert\mathcal{F}_{f(e)} - f\right\rVert_{I_e}\]
    For a given $\delta \in \mathbb{Q}^+$ such that $\delta < \frac{1}{2}$, the approximation $\mathcal{F}$ is said to be: 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \emph{$(I, \delta)$ admissible} if $\left\lVert\mathcal{F}\right\rVert_I < \delta$.
        \item \emph{provably} $(I, \delta)$ admissible if $\bigwedge_{f(e) \in \text{Term}_{\text{F}}(\varphi)} \left\lVert\mathcal{F}_{f(e)} - f\right\rVert_{I_e} < \delta$ is provable (in $\text{\upshape\textsf{d{\kern-0.05em}L}}\xspace$).
    \end{itemize}
    A sequence of approximants $(\mathcal{F}_{\delta_i})_i$ with $\delta_i \rightarrow 0$ is said to be (provably) \emph{$I$ admissible} if for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathcal{F}_{\delta_i}$ is (provably) $(I, \delta_i)$ admissible. For brevity, such sequences are indexed as $(\mathcal{F}_\delta)_\delta$ with the understanding that $\delta \rightarrow 0$ and $\delta_i < \frac{1}{2}$.
head: environment
name: Admissible approximations

title: Remark
body_md: The notion of admissibility introduced in Definition \ref{def: admissible approximants} requires $\left\lVert\mathcal{F}\right\rVert_I < \delta$, which is slightly stronger than the premise of $\left\lVert\mathcal{F}\right\rVert_I \leq \delta$ appearing in Theorem \ref{thm: proof rules for delta perturbations}. This difference arises to allow for a more uniform treatment of robustness in Section \ref{sec: robustness}.

    There is a computable algorithm that takes in bounded sentences $\varphi \in \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$, rational constants $\delta > 0$ and outputs the following:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item A bounded sentence $\mathcal{A}^\forall(\varphi, \delta) \in \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$, the ``$\delta$ strengthening'' of $\varphi$.
        
        \item The corresponding truth value of $\mathcal{A}^\forall(\varphi, \delta)$.
        
        \item In the case that $\mathcal{A}^\forall(\varphi, \delta)$ is true, a proof of $\varphi$ being true in $\text{\upshape\textsf{d{\kern-0.05em}L}}\xspace$.  
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Proof-producing $\delta$-decidability

title: Remark
body_md: Theorem \ref{thm: delta decidability with proofs} is precisely what this article means by ``$\delta$-decidability'' with proofs. Output (1) of the algorithm is a purely syntactic modification of the sentence, output (2) decides the truth value of the perturbed $\text{FOL}_{\mathbb{R}}$ sentence, for which there are existing proof-generating decision procedures \cite{DBLP:conf/cade/McLaughlinH05}. In the case that the $\delta$ strengthening of $\varphi$ is true, output (3) further produces a \emph{symbolic proof} in $\text{\upshape\textsf{d{\kern-0.05em}L}}\xspace$ of the truth of $\varphi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The proof of Theorem \ref{thm: delta decidability with proofs} proves something stronger, that \emph{every} $(I, \delta)$ admissible approximation $\mathcal{F}$ gives rise to a $\delta$ decision procedure. For future works it would be interesting to determine the most useful approximations for domain-specific problems.

label: def: pure formulas
title: Definition
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{def: pure formulas}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    A formula $\varphi \in \text{Fml}(\mathcal{L}_C)$ is said to be \emph{pure} if its normal form only contains one type of relation symbol $\succeq~\in \{\geq, >\}$, in which case it is also said to be $\succeq$-pure.
head: environment
name: Pure formulas

label: def: bounded semantics
title: Definition
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{def: bounded semantics}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\varphi(\vec{x}) \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)$ be a bounded formula of arity $n$ ($\lvertFV(\varphi)\rvert = n$) and $D : FV(\varphi) \to \mathbb{I}\mathbb{Q}$ a domain of $\varphi$. The \emph{bounded semantics} of $\varphi$ relative to $D$, $\left\llbracket \varphi(\vec{x}) \right\rrbracket_{D}$, is defined as
    \[\left\llbracket \varphi(\vec{x}) \right\rrbracket_{D} = D \cap \left\llbracket \varphi(\vec{x}) \right\rrbracket = \{\vec{y} \in \left\llbracket \varphi(\vec{x}) \right\rrbracket~\vert~\forall 1 \leq i \leq n(y_i \in D_{x_i})\}\]
    Correspondingly, write $D \models \varphi(\vec{x})$ if and only if $\left\llbracket \varphi(\vec{x}) \right\rrbracket_{D} = D$. If $\varphi$ is a sentence and $FV(\varphi) = \emptyset$, we define $\left\llbracket \varphi \right\rrbracket_{D} = \left\llbracket \varphi \right\rrbracket \in \{\top, \bot\}$ to be the truth value of $\varphi$.
head: environment
name: Bounded semantics

label: def: robustness
title: Definition
head: environment
name: Robustness

title: Remark
body_md:
By definition, the set of robust sentences (note that this does not depend on a choice of domain since sentences have no free variables) is 
    \[\{\varphi \in \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)~\vert~\text{$\varphi$ is $\forall$-robust}\}\]
    It is natural to consider a different notion of robustness where a sentence $\varphi$ is said to be robust if it satisfies at least one of the requirements in Definition \ref{def: robustness}, the set of robust sentences would then be
    \[\{\varphi \in \text{Sent}_{\text{B}}(\mathcal{L}_D)~\vert~\text{$\varphi$ is $\forall$-robust or $\exists$-robust}\}\]
    However since every true sentence is trivially $\exists$-robust and every false sentence is trivially $\forall$-robust, this would imply that all sentences are either $\exists$-robust or $\forall$-robust, trivializing the definition.

label: ex: non-robust formula
title: Example
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{ex: non-robust formula}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Consider the true sentence 
    \[\varphi \equiv \forall^{[0, 1]}x \left(e^x - 1 > 0 \textbar \left(1 - e^x \geq 0 \& e^x - 1 \geq 0\right)\right)\]
    note that $e^x$ is indeed differentially definable via the IVP $y' = y, y(0) = 1$ with provable global existence since its corresponding ODE is linear \cite{DBLP:journals/fac/TanP21}. For all $0 < \delta < \frac{1}{2}$, let $p_\delta(x)$ be a polynomial satisfying $\left\lVertp_\delta(x) - e^x\right\rVert_{[0, 1]} < \delta$ and $p_\delta(0) = 1$ (e.g. Taylor expansion of sufficiently high degree) so that the sequence of approximations $(e^x \mapsto p_\delta(x))_\delta$ is $I$ admissible where $I$ is the enclosure of $\varphi$ defined by $I_x = [0, 1], I_{e^x} = [0, 3]$ (since $e^x$ is not the argument of any other function term, the value of $I_{e^x}$ can be assigned arbitrarily and has no effect). For any $\delta$, the corresponding perturbation is then
    \[\mathcal{A}^\forall_{e^x \mapsto p_\delta(x)}(\varphi, \delta) \equiv \forall^{[0, 1]}x \forall w \left(\lvertw - p_\delta(x)\rvert \leq \delta \rightarrow w - 1 > 0 \textbar \left(1 - w \geq 0 \& w - 1 \geq 0\right)\right)\]
    which is not satisfied at $x = 0, w = 1 - \frac{\delta}{2}$, and therefore the perturbed sentence is false. Since this construction works for all $\delta > 0$, Theorem \ref{thm: chacterization of robustness} shows that $\varphi$ is not $\forall$-robust. Furthermore, Lemma \ref{lem: perturbation of negated formulas} implies that $\neg \varphi$ will not be $\exists$-robust.

name: Non-robust sentence

label: thm: atomic formulas are robust
title: Theorem
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{thm: atomic formulas are robust}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\succeq~\in \{\geq, >\}$ be a relation symbol and $\varphi \in \text{Fml}_B^\succeq(\mathcal{L}_D)$ a bounded $\succeq$-pure formula, then:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $\succeq = >$, then $\varphi$ is $\forall$-robust relative to all domains.
        \item If $\succeq = \geq$, then $\varphi$ is $\exists$-robust relative to all domains. 
    \end{itemize}
head: environment
name: Pure formulas are robust

label: lem: continuously choose interior
title: Lemma
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{lem: continuously choose interior}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\varphi \in \text{Fml}^{>}_B(\mathcal{L}_D)$ be a bounded formula of arity $n$. There exists a continuous function $r_\varphi : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}$ such that the following are equivalent for all $\vec{z} \in \mathbb{R}^n$:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\vec{z} \in \left\llbracket \varphi \right\rrbracket$
        \item $r_\varphi(\vec{z}) > 0$
        \item $r_\varphi(\vec{z}) > 0$ and $B(\vec{z}, r_\varphi(\vec{z})) \subseteq \left\llbracket \varphi \right\rrbracket$, where $B(\vec{z}, r_\varphi(\vec{z}))$ denotes the open ball of radius $r_\varphi(\vec{z})$ centered at $\vec{z}$. 
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to show that $\left\llbracket \varphi \right\rrbracket$ is an open set, since then $r_\varphi$ can be taken to be the distance function to $\left\llbracket \neg \varphi \right\rrbracket$ and the claim follows. First note that one can find some bounded formula $\psi \equiv \varphi$ such that $\psi$ only quantifies over $[0, 1]$, and it suffices to prove the claim for $\psi$ as $\left\llbracket \varphi \right\rrbracket = \left\llbracket \psi \right\rrbracket$. We will prove the claim for $\psi$ by induction, noting that the base case for atomic formulas follow directly by continuity of terms. Suppose $\psi(x) \equiv\forall^{[0, 1]}y~\eta(x, y)$, giving
    \[\left\llbracket \psi \right\rrbracket = \{x \in \mathbb{R}~\vert~\forall^{[0, 1]}y~(x, y) \in \left\llbracket \eta \right\rrbracket\} = \left(\text{Proj}(\left\llbracket \eta \right\rrbracket^c \cap (\mathbb{R}^n \times [0, 1]))\right)^c\]
    where $\mathbb{R}^n$ is viewed as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ representing the first $n$-coordinates. By induction, $\left\llbracket \eta \right\rrbracket$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ and therefore $\left\llbracket \eta \right\rrbracket^c \cap (\mathbb{R}^n \times [0, 1])$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n \times [0, 1]$. Since $[0, 1]$ is compact, the natural projection $\text{Proj} : \mathbb{R}^n \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a closed map, and therefore $\text{Proj}(\left\llbracket \eta \right\rrbracket^c \cap (\mathbb{R}^n \times [0, 1]))$ is a closed set in $\mathbb{R}^n$, consequently $\left\llbracket \psi \right\rrbracket$ is open. The dual case of existential quantification holds similarly, noting that $\text{Proj}$ is always an open map. And the case for logical connectives correspond to finite unions/intersections and are therefore trivial. Thus, the proof follows by induction.

    \[\mathbf{0}^{(\omega)} = \{<#n, k>#~\vert~n \in \mathbf{0}^{(k)}\}\]

title: Definition
body_md:
For sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, we say $A \leq_m B$ ($A$ is $m$-reducible to $B$) if there is a computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$:
    \[n \in A \iff f(n) \in B\]

label: lem: encode predicates as formulas
title: Lemma
body_md:
\if@filesw\immediate\write\@auxout 
   {\string\newlabel{lem: encode predicates as formulas}{{\arabic{HilbertRuleAppCounter}}{\thepage}}}\fi
    Let $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to [0, 1)$ be the function defined by $\alpha(n) = 1 - 2^{-n}$. There exists a computable function that takes in computable predicates $R \subseteq \mathbb{N}^n$ and outputs corresponding formulas $\varphi_R(\vec{x}) \in \text{Fml}_B(\mathcal{L}_C)$ of the same arity such that for all $\vec{m} \in \mathbb{N}^n$, we have:
    \[R(\vec{m}) \iff \mathbb{R}_C \models \varphi_R(\alpha(\vec{m}))\]
    Where $\alpha(\vec{m}) = (\alpha(\vec{m}_1), \cdots, \alpha(\vec{m}_n))$, and $R(\vec{m})$ denotes $\vec{m} \in R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: See Appendix \ref{app: proofs}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to (effectively) interpret $\langle \mathbb{N}, 0, 1, +, \cdot \rangle$. That is, it is sufficient to establish the following:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists some injection $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to [0, 1]$ such that its image $\alpha[\mathbb{N}]$ and $\alpha(0), \alpha(1)$ are all definable in $\mathbb{R}_C$ with bounded formulas.
        \item A formula $\text{Add}(x, y, z) \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathbb{R}_C)$ such that for all $n_1, n_2, n_3 \in \mathbb{N}$
        \[n_1 + n_2 = n_3 \iff (\alpha(n_1), \alpha(n_2), \alpha(n_3)) \in \left\llbracket \text{Add} \right\rrbracket\]

        \item A formula $\text{Mult}(x, y, z) \in \text{Fml}_{\text{B}}(\mathbb{R}_C)$ such that for all $n_1, n_2, n_3 \in \mathbb{N}$
        \[n_1 \cdot n_2 = n_3 \iff (\alpha(n_1), \alpha(n_2), \alpha(n_3)) \in \left\llbracket \text{Mult} \right\rrbracket\]
    \end{enumerate}
    The existence of such constructs would imply $\mathbf{0}^{(\omega)} \equiv_m \text{Th}(\mathbb{N}) \leq_m \text{Th}_{\text{B}}(\mathbb{R}_C)$ as desired. Note that by defining $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to [0, 1]$ as $\alpha(n) = 1 - 2^{-n}$, conditions (2), (3) are automatically satisfied by Lemma \ref{lem: encode predicates as formulas}, and $\alpha(0) = 0, \alpha(1) = \frac{1}{2}$ are both definable constants in $\mathbb{R}_C$. Thus, it remains to show that the image $\alpha[\mathbb{N}] \subseteq [0, 1]$ is definable using bounded formulas. First construct a computable function $g : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ as follows:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, define $g(\alpha(n)) = 0$.
        \item For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, set $g\left(\frac{\alpha(n) + \alpha(n + 1)}{2}\right) = 2^{-n}$. Then linearly interpolate over the intervals $\left[\alpha(n), \frac{\alpha(n) + \alpha(n + 1)}{2}\right]$ and $\left[\frac{\alpha(n) + \alpha(n + 1)}{2}, \alpha(n + 1)\right]$. As linear interpolation is computable, this defines a computable function $g: [0, 1) \to [0, 1]$.
        \item Define $g(1) = 0$. Note that for all $n$, for all $x \in [\alpha(n), 1)$, $g(x) \leq 2^{-n}$ by construction. In particular, this yields a computable modulus of continuity at $x = 1$, and therefore $g : [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ is a computable function \cite{Weihrauch_2000}.
    \end{itemize}
    Since $\mathcal{L}_C$ only permits total computable functions, take $h: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ to be some computable extension of $g$ \cite[ Expansion~theorem]{Pour-El_Richards_2017}. $\alpha[\mathbb{N}]$ can now be defined as follows to complete the proof
    \[\forall^{[0, 1]}x~x \in \alpha[\mathbb{N}] \iff (x \neq 1 \& h(x) = 0)\qedhere\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R \subseteq \mathbb{N}^n$ be a computable predicate. First construct a computable function $f: [0, 1]^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $f(\alpha(\vec{m})) > 0 \iff R(\vec{m})$ as follows:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For $\vec{m} \in \mathbb{N}^n$, define $f(\alpha(\vec{m})) = \frac{1}{\left\lVert\vec{m}\right\rVert}\chi_{R}(\vec{m})$, where $\left\lVert\vec{m}\right\rVert$ denotes the standard Euclidean norm, and $\chi_R : \mathbb{N}^n \to \{0, 1\}$ is the characteristic function of $R$. I.e. $\chi_R(\vec{m}) = 1 \iff \vec{m} \in R$.

        \item As $([\alpha(i), \alpha(i + 1)))_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ forms a partition of $[0, 1)$, it follows that $\left(\prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} [\alpha(\vec{m}_i), \alpha(\vec{m}_i + 1))\right)_{\vec{m} \in \mathbb{N}^n}$ forms a partition of $[0, 1)^n$. For each box of the form $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} [\alpha(\vec{m}_i), \alpha(\vec{m}_i + 1))$, define $f$ on $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} [\alpha(\vec{m}_i), \alpha(\vec{m}_i + 1))$ by multilinear interpolation from the vertices. I.e. For $\vec{x} \in \prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} [\alpha(\vec{m}_i), \alpha(\vec{m}_i + 1))$, $f(\vec{x})$ is the weighted average of the values of $f$ at the vertices of the box $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} [\alpha(\vec{m}_i), \alpha(\vec{m}_i + 1))$, which are already defined, note that this interpolation procedure is computable. Doing this for all boxes defines a computable function $f: [0, 1)^n \to \mathbb{R}$. 

        \item For $\vec{x} \in [0, 1]^n \setminus [0, 1)^n$, define $f(\vec{x}) = 0$. Note that this preserves the continuity of $f$, since for any sequence of points $(z_k)_k \to \vec{x}$ with $(z_k)_k \subseteq [0, 1)^n$, it is necessarily the case that the vectors $\vec{m}$ in part (1) of the construction which forms the vertices of the box that $z_i$ belongs to diverges to $\infty$ in norm. From this it follows by construction that $f(z_i)_i \to 0$. 
        
        It remains to verify that $f$ is still computable. To this end, let $\vec{x} \in [0, 1]^n$ be arbitrary, $(\vec{q}_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathbb{Q}^n$ be a name of $\vec{x}$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ be arbitrary. To prove that $f$ is computable, it suffices to (uniformly) compute some $q \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $\lvertq - f(\vec{x})\rvert < 2^{-k}$. This can be achieved by first searching for some finite index $n_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that at least one of the following is true:
            \begin{itemize}
                \item $B(\vec{q}_{n_1}, 2^{-n_1}) \cap [0, 1]^n \subseteq [0, 1)^n$ I.e. $\vec{q}_{n_1}$ witnesses $\vec{x} \in [0, 1)^n$, $f(\vec{x})$ can then be computed by the computable procedure in construction (2).

                \item For all $\vec{y} \in B(\vec{q}_{n_1}, 2^{-n_1}) \cap [0, 1)^n$, it is the case that $\left\lVert\vec{m}\right\rVert > 2^{k}$, where $\vec{m} \in \mathbb{N}^n$ characterizes the box that $\vec{y}$ belongs to in the sense of (2). In this case, we can simply output the desired value $q$ as $q = 0$. This is because $\vec{x} \in B(\vec{q}_{n_1}, 2^{-n_1})$, so either $\vec{x} \in [0, 1]^n \setminus [0, 1)^n$, in which case $f(\vec{x})$ is defined to be $0$. Or $\vec{x} \in B(\vec{q}_{n_1}, 2^{-n_1}) \cap [0, 1)^n$, so the value of $f$ at the vertices of $\vec{x}$ will all be smaller than $2^{-k}$ as $f(\vec{x}) \leq \frac{1}{\left\lVert\vec{m}\right\rVert} < 2^{-k}$.
            \end{itemize}
        It therefore remains to show that such an $n_1$ exists. Notice that if $\vec{x} \in [0, 1)^n$ holds, then some such $n_1$ necessarily exists. So suppose that $\vec{x} \in [0, 1]^n \setminus [0, 1)^n$, then the sequence $\vec{q}_n$ converges to some element in $[0, 1]^n \setminus [0, 1)^n$. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that the second condition does not hold for all $n_1$, then this gives a sequence $(\vec{y}_i)_i \subseteq [0, 1)^n$ converging to $\vec{x}$ such that the norms $\left\lVert\vec{m}_i\right\rVert$ does not diverge where $\vec{m}_i \in \mathbb{N}^n$ are the corners of $\vec{y}_i$'s, contradicting the construction of $\alpha(\vec{m})$. Hence, such a $n_1$ necessarily exists, and the search is therefore computable. 
    \end{enumerate} 
    The construction yields a computable function $f : [0, 1]^n \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $R(\vec{m}) \iff f(\alpha(\vec{m})) > 0$. However, recall that $\mathcal{L}_C$ only allows for univariate functions, yet $f$ is $n$-ary. To this end, let $\rho : [0, 1] \to [0, 1]^n$ denote the computable space-filling curve given by Lemma \ref{lem: space-filling curve}, and denote by $\rho_i$ the natural (computable) projections for $1 \leq i \leq n$. As $f$ is computable, it follows that the function $h \coloneqq f \circ \rho : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ is computable as well. Without loss of generality, we may further computably extend $h$'s domain to all of $\mathbb{R}$ \cite[Extension Theorem]{Pour-El_Richards_2017}. It then follows by construction that the following equivalences hold:
    \[R(\vec{m}) \iff f(\alpha(\vec{m})) > 0 \iff \exists^{[0, 1]}y \left(\bigwedge_{1 \leq i \leq n} \rho_i(y) = \alpha_i(\vec{m}) \& h(y) > 0\right)\]
    which is a bounded formula in the language $\mathcal{L}_C$, completing the proof.
head: environment
name: Proof of Lemma \ref{lem: encode predicates as formulas}
